b. Notable Early Constitutional Controversies Outside the 
Courts
The scope of presidential authority to supervise the Executive 
Branch—and thus, by implication, the scope of presidential removal 
power—^has been a subject of constitutional debate dating back to the First 
Congress. The topic went virtually undiscussed at either the Philadelphia 
Convention or state ratifying conventions. And because the Constitution 
says nothing about the removal of officers other than through 
impeachment, disputes have necessarily focused on inferences to be drawn 
from more general constitutional grants of authority to the President and 
to Congress. On the one hand. Article 11 of the Constitution vests the 
“executive Power” in the President, requires that he “take Care that the 
Laws be faithfully executed,” and vests the chief executive with 
appointment power over all principal officers. On the other hand. Article I 
gives Congress the power “[t]o make all Laws which shall be necessary and 
proper for carrying into Execution ... all [ ] Powers vested by this 
Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any Department 
. .. thereof’—^which presumably includes at least some authority to 
organize and control the bureaucracy.
Between 1789 and 1926, however, the Supreme Court avoided issuing 
an authoritative ruling on the question. The Court’s relative silence thus 
left it to the elected branches of government to joust—^both internally and 
with one another—over the scope of presidential removal authority, a 
dispute that surfaced repeatedly in some of the era’s most significant 
political episodes.
Creating the First Departments, Debating in the First Congress, 
different Members held the various positions (1) that the Constitution 
guaranteed the president plenary removal power, (2) that presidents could 
remove officers only to the extent authorized by Congress, or (3) that 
presidents could remove officers—at least Senate-confirmod officers—only 
with the Senate’s consent to removal. (The last was the position Alexander 
Hamilton espoused in the FederaUst, No. 77, an opinion he appeared to 
change in favor of plenary removal power during his tenure as George 
Washington’s Treasury Secretary.) In what came to be known as “the 
Decision of 1789,” the House of Representatives struck language in the 
statute creating the Department of Foreign Affairs that would have made 
the Secretary explicitly “removable by the President.” The House 
substituted statutory language that presupposed that the President could 
remove heads of departments, although the text did not specify the source 
of that power. Those who interpret the Constitution as giving the President 
plenary power—^most notably Chief Justice Taft in the Myers case, 
discussed infra—^regard the statutory change as evidence of a congressional 
decision in favor of a constitutionally-based plenary presidential removal 
power. See Aditya Bamzai & Saikrishna Bangalore Prakash, The Executive
